planting.note: Set out container-grown saplings in spring once frost danger has passed, in a site with excellent drainage.

directions: Quillaja saponaria, the soap bark tree, is an evergreen sclerophyll tree native to the Chilean matorral, where tough, leathery leaves and a deep root system let it endure long dry Mediterranean-climate summers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water regularly only while the tree is establishing; mature specimens need little supplemental irrigation and handle periodic drought well. Small white flower clusters in late spring are followed by distinctive five-parted woody seed capsules that split open into a star shape as they dry. The inner bark is naturally rich in saponins and has long been harvested commercially for soap, shampoo, and as a foaming agent in beverages, so avoid siting it where children might peel or chew the bark.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Transplant nursery-grown saplings in spring into well-drained soil, watering regularly until roots establish.

directions: Cryptocarya alba, known as peumo, is an evergreen laurel-family tree native to the central Chilean matorral and adjoining sclerophyll woodland, forming a dense, rounded canopy of glossy, leathery leaves. Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, watering regularly during establishment; once mature it tolerates the long dry summers typical of its native Mediterranean climate. Small greenish-yellow flowers in spring are followed by egg-shaped drupes that ripen deep red-purple; the fresh fruit is astringent and is traditionally boiled before eating rather than consumed raw. Slow-growing and long-lived, peumo is planted in Chile both as an ornamental shade tree and for erosion control on dry slopes.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery stock after all frost danger has passed, in a warm, humid, sheltered spot.

directions: Fagraea berteroana, called pua kenikeni in Hawaii and grown across the tropical Pacific including French Polynesia, is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree prized for its intensely fragrant flowers. The waxy, tubular blossoms open creamy white in the evening and deepen to golden orange over several days, filling the garden with a sweet scent reminiscent of gardenia and citrus blossom. Plant in full sun to light shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil and water regularly, since it tolerates neither prolonged drought nor frost. Flowers are traditionally strung into leis once they age to deep orange, and the plant is widely grown as a dooryard shrub or hedge in Pacific island gardens for that purpose.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in warm weather once frost risk has fully passed, in sandy, fast-draining soil.

directions: Pandanus tectorius, called hala in Hawaii and fara in Tahiti, is an iconic Pacific Island tree known for its spirally arranged, sword-like leaves and distinctive stilt (prop) roots that brace the trunk above ground. It thrives in full sun on sandy or rocky coastal soils and tolerates salt spray, wind, and drought once established, making it well suited to seaside tropical landscapes. The species is dioecious: male plants produce fragrant flower spikes historically used in Polynesian leis and scent-making, while female plants bear large, pineapple-like aggregate fruits composed of many fibrous segments. Across Polynesia the long, spine-edged leaves are stripped, dried, and woven into mats, baskets, and thatch, making this planting both ornamental and culturally significant.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
